🏭 Production GPU Infrastructure — SRE's 6 Pillars

Running NVIDIA AI in production requires these six operational pillars:

  1. SECURITY: Scanned containers, MIG isolation, Vault secrets, air-gapped BMC/IPMI
  2. COST: MIG (split GPU), spot instances (60-90% cheaper), autoscale to zero at night
  3. HA/DR: Multi-AZ Triton, 3-tier checkpoints (NVMe+S3+cross-region), RTO <5 min
  4. COMPLIANCE: MLflow audit trail, model cards, data lineage, RBAC
  5. UPGRADES: Rolling drain → upgrade → dcgmi diag → uncordon (zero downtime)
  6. MONITORING: DCGM→Prometheus→Grafana→PagerDuty, daily health scripts

📝 NVIDIA Practice Questions — Chapter 29

Q1

What is MIG and how does it improve GPU utilization?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) partitions an A100 or H100 into up to 7 isolated GPU instances, each with dedicated memory, cache, and compute units. This enables running multiple workloads on one GPU simultaneously with hardware-level isolation — no cross-tenant data leakage. Improves utilization by allowing smaller jobs (inference, dev) to share a GPU without interfering with each other.

💡 EXPLANATION

MIG = hardware GPU partitioning. A100/H100 → up to 7 isolated slices with dedicated SM + memory.

  Before MIG: 1 GPU = 1 workload. After: 1 H100 = 7 isolated workloads.
  Hardware-enforced at SM & memory controller. Slice 1 OOM can't affect slice 2.
  🎯 anihpj: 4 MIG slices → dev, test, staging, prod Triton ALL on one H100.
Q2

What security measures should protect GPU infrastructure?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Container scanning (Trivy/Grype on all images), MIG for GPU isolation (hard multi-tenancy), non-root containers with seccomp/AppArmor, network segmentation (GPU traffic on isolated VLANs), secrets in Vault/SealedSecrets (never hardcode NGC keys), no internet exposure for GPU management interfaces (BMC/IPMI), Triton authentication (API keys or mTLS).

💡 EXPLANATION

7-layer defense: scan images, MIG isolate, non-root, VLAN segment, vault secrets, air-gap BMC, auth Triton.

  Container scan (Trivy) → MIG isolation (hard walls) → non-root + seccomp → VLAN segment
  → Vault secrets (no hardcoded keys) → BMC/IPMI air-gapped → Triton API keys/mTLS
  🎯 GPU processes PII/models. Compromised container = IP theft + data breach. Defense in depth.
Q3

How can GPU costs be reduced in production?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

MIG: split one GPU into multiple instances. Spot instances: 60-90% cheaper for fault-tolerant training. Right-sizing: L4 for inference ($0.40/h), H100 for training ($12/h). Autoscaling: scale to zero at night. Reserved instances: 40-60% discount for baseline capacity. MPS: share GPU across small jobs. Combined: anihpj achieves ~55% cost reduction vs all on-demand H100s.

💡 EXPLANATION

Match GPU tier to workload. Right-size + spot + reserved + autoscale = ~55% cost reduction.

  MIG: 1 GPU → 7 slices (+50% util). Spot: 60-90% off for batch training.
  Right-size: L40S ($1.5/h) for inference, H100 ($12/h) for training.
  Reserved: 40-60% off baseline. Autoscale to zero at night.
  🎯 anihpj: H100(train) + L40S(infer) + spot(batch) + reserved(baseline) = 55% savings.
Q4

How do you achieve high availability for Triton Inference Server?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Deploy multiple Triton pods across 3 availability zones behind a Layer 7 load balancer. Each pod serves the same model versions from a shared model repository (S3/NFS). Health checks at /v2/health/ready. If one AZ fails, the load balancer routes traffic to healthy pods in other AZs — zero interruption. Kubernetes HPA scales pods based on request latency or GPU utilization.

💡 EXPLANATION

Triton HA: 3 AZs, shared model repo (S3), /v2/health/ready health check, HPA autoscaling.

  Triton pod (AZ-1) ─┐
  Triton pod (AZ-2) ─┼─ L7 LB → Django clients. S3 model repo shared across all pods.
  Triton pod (AZ-3) ─┘
  Health: /v2/health/ready → 200 only if models loaded. 503 → LB stops traffic. Auto-recovery.
  🎯 AZ-1 fails → LB routes to AZ-2/3. Users never notice. New model: update S3 path → reload.
Q5

What is the GPU cluster upgrade strategy with zero downtime?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Rolling upgrades with GPU Operator on K8s: (1) Cordon one GPU node — no new workloads scheduled. (2) Drain node — GPU Operator migrates existing workloads to healthy GPUs. (3) Upgrade GPU driver/CUDA on the drained node. (4) Run diagnostic test (dcgmi diag -r 1) to verify GPU health. (5) Uncordon node — workloads can now schedule. (6) Repeat for each node. For anihpj: ~10 min per DGX, ~1 hour for all 4 nodes, zero workload downtime.

💡 EXPLANATION

Rolling upgrade: cordon → drain (GPU Operator migrates) → upgrade driver → dcgmi diag → uncordon.

  1. kubectl cordon      → No new workloads
  2. kubectl drain        → GPU Operator auto-migrates to healthy GPUs
  3. Upgrade driver/CUDA        → ~10 min per DGX
  4. dcgmi diag -r 1            → Quick GPU health check (<2 min)
  5. kubectl uncordon     → Only if diag passes. If fail → investigate.
  🎯 anihpj: 4 DGX × 10 min = ~1 hour total. Zero workload downtime.
Q6

What MLflow features support AI compliance and governance?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

MLflow Tracking: Records every training run — hyperparameters, metrics, GPU config, dataset version, code commit hash. MLflow Model Registry: Versioned models with stage transitions (Staging→Production→Archived), each logged with who/when/why. Artifact storage: Model files + environment + evaluation results. These together provide the audit trail required for SOC 2, ISO 27001, and FDA AI/ML compliance.

💡 EXPLANATION

MLflow = audit trail for AI. Tracking (who/when/config), Registry (approval gates), Artifacts (data lineage).

  Tracking: hyperparams + GPU config + dataset hash + code commit. Every run recorded.
  Registry: Staging→Production→Archived transitions with who/when/why. Manual approval gates.
  Artifacts: Model files + env + eval results. Data lineage via dataset hash.
  🎯 SOC 2: need change mgmt → Registry approvals. FDA: need data lineage → dataset hashes.
Q7

What is the disaster recovery strategy for AI training jobs?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Three-tier checkpoint storage: (1) Local NVMe — fastest restore, (2) S3/GCS in primary region — durable, (3) S3/GCS in secondary region — DR. Training jobs save checkpoints every N steps. If a GPU fails: GPU Operator detects the failure, the K8s Job restarts on a healthy GPU, PyTorch loads the latest checkpoint, and training resumes from that point. Typical progress loss: <5 minutes of training.

Q8

What is the difference between MIG and MPS?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU): Hardware-level partitioning — creates truly isolated GPU instances with dedicated memory, cache, SM units. Best for: hard multi-tenancy, different users/teams, security isolation. MPS (Multi-Process Service): Software-level sharing — allows multiple CUDA contexts to run concurrently on one GPU with configurable resource limits. Best for: soft sharing within one tenant, multiple small experiments on one GPU. MIG = hardware isolation, MPS = software sharing.

💡 EXPLANATION

MIG = hardware isolation (apartment walls). MPS = software sharing (room dividers).

  MIG: Dedicated SM + memory per slice. OOM can't cross. For multi-tenant, security-critical.
  MPS: Multiple CUDA contexts share GPU. Configurable limits. For same-team experiments, efficiency.
  🎯 MIG = hard walls. MPS = soft dividers. Choose based on isolation vs utilization trade-off.

30.2 NVIDIA in Quantum Computing — cuQuantum

NVIDIA isn't building quantum computers — but they're building the simulators that make quantum computing practical. cuQuantum is an SDK of optimized libraries (cuStateVec, cuTensorNet) for simulating quantum circuits on NVIDIA GPUs.

❌ CPU Simulation (Impossible at Scale)

A 30-qubit circuit requires a state vector of 2³⁰ = 1,073,741,824 complex numbers. That's 16GB just for the state vector — and every gate operation touches all of them. 35+ qubits is completely infeasible on any CPU. Researchers without GPU simulation must wait for scarce, expensive quantum hardware.

✅ GPU Simulation (cuQuantum)

cuStateVec: State vector simulation on GPU — 30+ qubits in minutes on H100. cuTensorNet: Tensor network contraction — handles 100+ qubit circuits with specific structure. Speedup: 10-100× vs CPU simulation. Available as DGX cuQuantum Appliance for national labs and quantum computing companies.

🎯 Why This Matters

Quantum hardware is scarce (IBM, Google, IonQ have a handful of machines), expensive ($1M+ per quantum processor), and noisy (error rates limit practical algorithms). cuQuantum lets researchers develop and test quantum algorithms on DGX GPUs today — then run the validated algorithms on real quantum hardware tomorrow. It's the quantum development workstation before the quantum computer exists. For NCA-AIIO: know that cuQuantum = GPU-accelerated quantum circuit simulation, not actual quantum computing.

30.4 Sustainable AI Computing

AI's energy consumption is a growing concern — but NVIDIA GPUs are dramatically more efficient than CPUs for AI. A single H100 delivers the same AI inference performance as ~25 CPU servers, using ~1/25th the energy. Liquid-cooled DGX systems reduce data center PUE from 1.6 (air-cooled) to below 1.1 (direct-to-chip liquid cooling). For anihpj: switching from CPU-based job matching to GPU-based (Triton on H100) reduces energy per query by 20× — good for both the planet and the electricity bill. NVIDIA's goal: accelerated computing is sustainable computing — do more work with less energy by using the right processor for the right task.

This bonus chapter covers critical topics from the official NVIDIA documentation and NCA-AIIO exam blueprint that may not fit neatly into earlier chapters. These are directly tested on the exam and essential for production NVIDIA deployments.

B.1 NVIDIA Run:ai — GPU Workload Scheduling & Resource Management

Run:ai (acquired by NVIDIA) is the GPU orchestration and scheduling platform included in NVIDIA AI Enterprise. It provides: GPU resource pooling (treat all cluster GPUs as one shared pool), fair-share scheduling with quotas and priorities, GPU fractions (run multiple workloads on one GPU), and both self-hosted and SaaS deployment options.

📖 Key Run:ai Concepts
  • Projects: Namespaces with GPU quotas — allocate X GPUs to Team A, Y GPUs to Team B
  • GPU Fractions: Time-slicing and MIG partitioning to share GPUs across workloads
  • Queue Management: Priority-based queuing — high-priority training jobs preempt lower-priority ones
  • Run:ai SaaS: NVIDIA-managed cloud control plane — included in NVAIE license, no self-hosting needed

Exam relevance: The NCA-AIIO AI Operations domain (22%) covers "cluster orchestration and job scheduling essentials." Know that Run:ai = GPU workload scheduling for K8s clusters.

B.1b Slurm — HPC Workload Manager for GPU Clusters

Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) is the dominant HPC workload manager used on bare-metal GPU clusters, including DGX SuperPOD. While Run:ai handles GPU scheduling on Kubernetes, Slurm is the standard for traditional HPC environments — national labs, research institutions, and enterprises running AI training on non-containerized bare-metal clusters. NVIDIA's Base Command Manager (BCM) integrates with Slurm for job queuing on DGX SuperPOD.

🔧 What Slurm Does

Slurm manages cluster resources and schedules jobs. It handles:
• Resource Allocation: Assigns GPUs, CPUs, memory to jobs
• Job Queuing: FIFO + priority-based queuing with preemption
• GPU-Aware Scheduling: Tracks which GPUs are free/busy per node
• Fair Share: Prevents one user/team from hogging all GPUs
• Accounting: Tracks GPU-hours per user/project for billing

📋 Key Slurm Commands

Every GPU cluster operator should know:
• sbatch job.sh — Submit a job script
• squeue — View job queue (running + pending)
• scancel <job_id> — Cancel a job
• sinfo — View node/partition status
• scontrol show job <job_id> — Detailed job info
• sacct — Job accounting/history
• srun --gpus=2 nvidia-smi — Run command with GPUs

🖥️ Slurm Partitions & GPU GRES

Slurm organizes nodes into partitions (queues). GPU clusters typically have:
• dgx partition: DGX nodes for large training jobs
• gpu partition: Single-GPU nodes for inference/dev
• cpu partition: CPU-only nodes for data prep
GPUs are configured as GRES (Generic Resources) in slurm.conf:
GresTypes=gpu
NodeName=dgx[01-04] Gres=gpu:8
Jobs request GPUs: #SBATCH --gres=gpu:4

⚖️ Slurm vs Kubernetes

When to use Slurm:
• Bare-metal GPU clusters (no containers)
• HPC-style batch processing
• Multi-user research environments
• When you need GPU GRES scheduling
When to use Kubernetes:
• Containerized AI workloads (NGC containers)
• Microservices-based inference
• Auto-scaling and rolling updates
• Multi-cloud/hybrid deployments
BCM bridges both: uses Slurm for job queuing on DGX SuperPOD.

📋 Slurm Job Lifecycle — From Submission to Completion
  SLURM GPU JOB LIFECYCLE
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. SUBMIT        2. QUEUED         3. RUNNING        4. COMPLETING      │
  │  ─────────        ─────────        ─────────        ──────────────      │
  │  $ sbatch          Job waits         GPUs allocated    Output saved      │
  │    train.sh         for GPUs          Model trains      to job.out       │
  │       │                │                  │                 │            │
  │       ▼                ▼                  ▼                 ▼            │
  │  ┌─────────┐     ┌─────────┐       ┌─────────┐      ┌─────────┐         │
  │  │ Job ID  │ ──▶ │ Priority│  ──▶  │ 4× H100 │ ──▶  │Complete │         │
  │  │ #12345  │     │ Queue   │       │ DGX-02  │      │ Exit:0  │         │
  │  └─────────┘     └─────────┘       └─────────┘      └─────────┘         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  KEY STATES: PD=Pending, R=Running, CG=Completing, F=Failed, CA=Cancelled│
  │  Check: squeue | watch squeue    Cancel: scancel 12345                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝 Example Slurm GPU Job Script for anihpj
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=anihpj-train       # Job name
  #SBATCH --partition=dgx               # Use DGX partition
  #SBATCH --nodes=2                     # 2 DGX nodes
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:8                  # 8 GPUs per node (16 total)
  #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1           # One task per node
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=32            # 32 CPU cores per task
  #SBATCH --mem=500G                    # 500 GB RAM per node
  #SBATCH --time=04:00:00               # Max 4 hours runtime
  #SBATCH --output=anihpj_%j.out       # Output file (job ID in name)
  #SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL          # Email on completion/failure

  # Load CUDA environment
  module load cuda/12.2

  # Run distributed training
  srun torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8 train_job_rec.py \
      --batch-size 256 --epochs 10 --data /data/anihpj/postings/

  echo "Training complete. Model saved to /models/anihpj/"

🔑 Exam Tip — Slurm

For NCA-AIIO, know: Slurm = HPC workload manager for bare-metal GPU clusters. Uses GRES for GPU scheduling. BCM integrates with Slurm on DGX SuperPOD. The exam won't ask detailed Slurm commands but expects you to know what Slurm IS and when you'd use it vs K8s. Key distinction: Slurm = traditional HPC/bare-metal, K8s = containerized, Run:ai = K8s-native GPU scheduling layer.

B.2 NVIDIA Network Operator & DOCA — DPU Ecosystem

The Network Operator is the sibling of the GPU Operator — it manages NVIDIA networking hardware (ConnectX NICs, BlueField DPUs, Spectrum switches) in Kubernetes. It automates: NIC driver installation, network configuration (RoCE, InfiniBand), and DPU provisioning.

DOCA (Data Center Infrastructure-on-a-Chip Architecture) is the SDK for programming BlueField DPUs. It provides libraries for: network acceleration (OVS, hairpin), storage acceleration (NVMe-oF, GPUDirect Storage), security (IPsec, TLS offload), and telemetry. Think of DOCA as "CUDA for DPUs" — the programming framework that makes DPUs useful.

Exam relevance: The exam asks "Explain the purpose and benefits of a DPU in a datacenter." Answer: DPUs offload infrastructure tasks (networking, storage, security) from the host CPU, freeing CPU cycles for AI workloads. DOCA is the programming model.

B.3 NVIDIA vGPU — GPU Virtualization for Virtual Machines

vGPU (Virtual GPU) enables multiple VMs to share a single physical GPU with guaranteed performance. Unlike MIG (hardware partitioning for containers), vGPU is designed for virtualized environments (VMware, Citrix, KVM).

FeatureMIG (Multi-Instance GPU)vGPU (Virtual GPU)
EnvironmentContainers (Kubernetes, Docker)Virtual Machines (VMware, KVM)
IsolationHardware-level (dedicated SM + memory)Software-level (NVIDIA driver scheduling)
GPUs SupportedA100, H100, B200Most data center GPUs
License TiersFree (built into GPU)vWS, vPC, vApps (NVAIE subscription)
Best ForMulti-tenant K8s AI inferenceVDI, virtual workstations

B.4 NVIDIA AI Enterprise Lifecycle — Branch Types

NVAIE uses a structured release system. Understanding branches is critical for production planning:

Branch TypeSupport WindowBest For
PB (Production Branch)9 months, monthly patchesLatest features, non-critical workloads
LTSB (Long-Term Support Branch)3 years, quarterly patchesProduction stability, regulated industries
FB (Feature Branch)Short-lived, rapid updatesEarly access to new features, testing
InfrastructureIndependent lifecycleGPU drivers, K8s operators (GPU Operator, Network Operator)

NVAIE 8.1 (FB/PB, 2026): GPU Driver 595.71.05, vGPU 20.1, Run:ai 2.25. NVAIE 7.5 (LTSB): GPU Driver 580.159.03, 3-year support through 2028.

B.5 NVIDIA Dynamo — Distributed Inference Serving

NVIDIA Dynamo is a data center-scale inference serving framework designed for complex generative AI use cases. While Triton handles single-node inference, Dynamo orchestrates inference across an entire cluster — disaggregating prefill and decode phases, managing KV-cache routing, and optimizing throughput across hundreds of GPUs.

Key features: Component-based architecture (mix-and-match serving components), disaggregated serving (separate prefill and decode across different GPUs), KV-cache-aware routing (send requests to the GPU that has the relevant KV-cache), and dynamic scaling. For anihpj: as the JD generator scales to serve thousands of concurrent users, Dynamo would optimize the LLM serving pipeline beyond what Triton alone can do.

B.6 NVIDIA AIStore & CUTLASS — Storage and Compute Libraries

NVIDIA AIStore: A deploy-anywhere distributed object store optimized for AI workloads. Provides linear scalability, seamless cloud-tiering (S3/GCS as backend), and native GPU data loading. Think "S3-compatible storage that understands GPU data pipelines."

NVIDIA CUTLASS: A collection of CUDA C++ template abstractions for implementing high-performance matrix multiplication (GEMM) and related computations. It's what powers much of cuBLAS and TensorRT under the hood. While most developers never touch CUTLASS directly, it's the foundation of NVIDIA's AI math performance.

B.7 NVIDIA Confidential Computing & DPX Instructions

NVIDIA Confidential Computing: H100 was the world's first accelerator with hardware-based trusted execution environment (TEE). It creates an isolated secure zone in the GPU where data and computation are protected — even from the host OS and hypervisor. This enables: multi-party AI training (multiple organizations train together without revealing their data), secure inference (protect proprietary models from theft), and compliance (HIPAA, GDPR data processing in a hardware-protected enclave). H100 and B200 both support Confidential Computing.

DPX Instructions: H100 introduces new Dynamic Programming X (DPX) instructions that accelerate dynamic programming algorithms — the class of algorithms used in DNA sequence alignment (Smith-Waterman), protein folding prediction, route optimization, and path planning. DPX delivers 7× higher performance over A100 and 40× over CPUs for these workloads. This is why H100 excels in life sciences and genomics — not just AI.

BQ1

What is NVIDIA Run:ai and how does it manage GPU resources?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Run:ai is NVIDIA's GPU orchestration platform (included in NVAIE). It pools all cluster GPUs into shared resources, provides fair-share scheduling with project quotas, supports GPU fractions (MIG + time-slicing), and offers both self-hosted and SaaS deployment. It's the scheduling layer on top of Kubernetes for AI workloads.

💡 EXPLANATION

Run:ai = GPU orchestration. Pool GPUs + fair-share scheduling + GPU fractions (MIG/time-slicing) + priority queues.

BQ2

What is the difference between MIG and vGPU?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

MIG: Hardware-level GPU partitioning for containers (K8s/Docker). Dedicated SM units and memory per instance. Free, built into A100/H100. vGPU: Software-level GPU sharing for virtual machines (VMware/KVM). NVIDIA driver manages GPU time-slicing across VMs. Requires NVAIE license.

💡 EXPLANATION

MIG: HW partitioning, containers, dedicated SM+memory, free. vGPU: SW sharing, VMs, driver time-slicing, NVAIE license.

  MIG (A100/H100): K8s/Docker. Hardware-isolated. Up to 7 instances. Free (built-in).
  vGPU (most GPUs): VMware/KVM. Software time-slicing. Flexible VM count. Needs NVAIE license.
  🎯 Containers→MIG. Virtual machines→vGPU. Exam: MIG=HW+containers, vGPU=SW+VMs.
BQ3

What are the three NVAIE branch types?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

PB (Production Branch): 9-month support, monthly patches. LTSB (Long-Term Support Branch): 3-year support, quarterly patches. FB (Feature Branch): Short-lived, rapid updates for early testing. Infrastructure components (drivers, operators) have independent lifecycle from application branches.

💡 EXPLANATION

PB (9mo, monthly patches), LTSB (3yr, quarterly patches), FB (short-lived, rapid). Infra = independent lifecycle.

  LTSB: Production stability, regulated industries. 3-year support. NVAIE 7.5 LTSB through 2028.
  PB: Latest features, non-critical. FB: Bleeding edge, testing only.
  🎯 Production → LTSB. Dev/staging → PB. CI test matrix → PB+LTSB.

What is NVIDIA Dynamo and how does it differ from Triton?

Click to reveal answer

Dynamo is a data center-scale distributed inference framework for generative AI. While Triton handles single-node model serving with dynamic batching, Dynamo orchestrates inference across HUNDREDS of GPUs — disaggregating prefill/decode phases, managing KV-cache routing across nodes, and optimizing cluster-wide throughput. Think Triton = single node, Dynamo = cluster.

💡 EXPLANATION

Dynamo = cluster-scale distributed inference. Disaggregates prefill/decode, KV-cache routing, 100s GPUs.

  Triton: single-node. Dynamic batching. Model ensembles. Best: <8 GPU inference.
  Dynamo: cluster-scale. Disaggregated prefill+decode. KV-cache-aware routing. Best: LLMs at 100+ GPUs.

What is DOCA and what role does it play with BlueField DPUs?

✅ ANSWER

DOCA (Data Center Infrastructure-on-a-Chip Architecture) is the SDK for programming BlueField DPUs — like "CUDA for DPUs." It provides libraries for network acceleration (OVS, RoCE), storage acceleration (NVMe-oF, GPUDirect Storage), security offload (IPsec, TLS), and telemetry. Before Diving Into Part 11 — Your SRE/PE Quick-Start Guide

📋 Daily SRE Tasks with GPU Infrastructure

🌅
Morning Health Check

nvidia-smi across all nodes. Check GPU utilization, memory, temp. dcgmi diag -r 1 quick diagnostic. Prometheus alerts review. Any XID errors overnight?

📊
Capacity Planning

GPU utilization trends. If >80% → plan expansion. If <50% → investigate idle GPUs. Monitor GPU memory pressure — OOM kills waste $100K+ GPU hours.

🔧
Troubleshooting GPUs

GPU falls off bus? dmesg | grep NVRM. XID 79/48? GPU may need RMA. ECC errors exceeding threshold? Schedule replacement. DCGM for proactive monitoring.

🔄
Maintenance Windows

Driver update: drain→cordon→update→reboot→uncordon→verify. Firmware: even more critical. Always test on non-production first. Automate with Ansible.

📈 GPU Monitoring — SRE Stack

Production GPU Monitoring Architecture
  GPU Nodes ──DCGM──▶ Prometheus ──▶ Grafana ──▶ Alertmanager
  (H100/A100)   50+ metrics    Dashboards:     → PagerDuty
                                GPU Util %      → Slack
                                GPU Mem GB      Alerts:
                                NVLink BW       • GPU temp >85°C
                                Power Watts     • XID Error detected
                                Throttling      • GPU offline
                                                • ECC > threshold
Prometheus Alert Rules — GPU SRE Critical
groups:
- name: gpu_sre_alerts
  rules:
  - alert: GPUOffline
    expr: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL == -1
    for: 2m
    annotations:
      summary: "GPU {{ $labels.gpu }} on {{ $labels.node }} OFFLINE"
  - alert: GPUThermalThrottling
    expr: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP > 85
    for: 5m
    annotations:
      summary: "GPU temp >85°C — throttling imminent"
  - alert: XIDError
    expr: increase(DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS[5m]) > 0
    annotations:
      summary: "XID error — potential GPU hardware failure"
  - alert: GPUMemoryHigh
    expr: DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED / DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_TOTAL > 0.95
    for: 10m
    annotations:
      summary: "GPU memory >95% — OOM risk"

🏗️ Infrastructure as Code — GPU Automation

📖 Platform Pattern: GPUs as Cattle, Not Pets

Every GPU node should be disposable. Automate with Terraform/Ansible. Never SSH into a GPU node for manual fixes — rebuild it. Immutable infrastructure.

Terraform — GPU Instance (AWS p5.48xlarge = 8x H100)
resource "aws_instance" "gpu_node" {
  ami           = "ami-nvidia-ubuntu-22.04"
  instance_type = "p5.48xlarge"  # 8x H100 GPUs
  user_data = templatefile("init.sh", {
    driver_ver = "550.54.15"
    cuda_ver   = "12.4"
  })
  tags = { GPU_Type = "H100", GPU_Count = "8" }
}

Spot/Preemptible GPUs

A100: training (312 TFLOPS, $3/hr). L40S: inference. H100: LLMs only ($30/hr). Match GPU to workload — don't overpay.

💡 SRE Insight: Why CUDA Knowledge Makes You a Better Troubleshooter

A traditional SRE seeing "GPU-Util at 100% but training is slow" would be stuck. An NVIDIA-trained SRE knows to check: (1) Are Tensor Cores actually being used? (ncu --set full), (2) Is the kernel memory-bound? (check SM efficiency vs memory throughput), (3) Is NCCL using NVLink or falling back to PCIe? (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO), (4) Are there bank conflicts in shared memory? (ncu --section MemoryWorkloadAnalysis). This depth is what separates a GPU SRE from a regular SRE — and it's exactly what this guide teaches.

31.2 GPU Cluster Lifecycle Management

GPU clusters have a lifecycle just like any infrastructure — but with unique challenges. A GPU node isn't a generic compute unit; it's a precision instrument with $240K worth of GPUs that need firmware updates, thermal management, and graceful degradation handling. This section covers the complete lifecycle from provisioning to decommissioning.

1
Provision

DGX unboxing, rack/stack, power/cooling verification, InfiniBand cabling, initial firmware baseline

2
Bootstrap

GPU Operator install, DCGM deploy, join K8s/Slurm cluster, NVLink topology validation

3
Operate

Workload scheduling, health monitoring, thermal/power tracking, driver/firmware patching

4
Maintain

Monthly maintenance windows, GPU RMA, NVLink re-seating, cooling system service

5
Decommission

GPU secure wipe, DGX de-racking, e-waste compliance, capacity replacement planning

Stage 1: Provision — From Crate to Cluster

Provisioning a DGX isn't like racking a standard server. Key differences every SRE must know:

⚡ Power Verification (STEP 1)

Before unboxing ANYTHING: Verify 3-phase 415V power is live at the rack. Each DGX H100 draws 10.2kW. A standard 208V single-phase circuit cannot power a DGX. Use a power quality analyzer to verify stable voltage under load. Budget 6-12 months lead time for data center power upgrades — start this BEFORE ordering DGX systems.

❄️ Cooling Verification (STEP 2)

Verify liquid cooling loop pressure (~1.5-2.0 bar), flow rate, and supply temperature (facility water at 32°C/90°F or below). Each DGX requires ~38 L/min coolant flow. Air cooling a DGX is NOT possible — the SXM GPUs have no fans, relying entirely on the cold plate loop. If your facility has only air cooling, you need a Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) per rack.

🔗 InfiniBand Cabling (STEP 3)

Each DGX has 8× InfiniBand ports (1 per GPU for GPUDirect RDMA). Cable mapping must follow the SuperPOD rail-optimized topology — GPU[i] on every DGX connects to the same IB leaf switch. One wrong cable = entire NCCL ring degraded. Use NVIDIA's cable validation script before joining the cluster. Label BOTH ends of every IB cable — you'll thank yourself during the first cable replacement at 3 AM.

✅ Acceptance Testing (STEP 4)

Run DCGM diagnostic level 3 (dcgmi diag -r 3) — this stresses GPU compute, memory, NVLink, and PCIe for 30+ minutes. Check: all GPUs pass, NVLink bandwidth within 5% of 900 GB/s per link, no thermal throttling, no ECC errors. Do NOT accept delivery without passing DCGM level 3. File any failures as DOA (Dead on Arrival) with NVIDIA within 48 hours.

Stage 2: Bootstrap — Software Stack Deployment

Once hardware is validated, deploy the GPU software stack. The GPU Operator automates this on Kubernetes — do NOT manually install drivers.

Bash — DGX Bootstrap Playbook (anihpj-dgx-bootstrap.sh)
#!/bin/bash
# anihpj-dgx-bootstrap.sh — DGX H100 node bootstrap for K8s GPU cluster
# Run on each DGX node as root (or via Ansible/PXE boot)

set -euo pipefail

echo "=== STEP 1: Verify Hardware ==="
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,serial,uuid,pcie.link.gen.current --format=csv
# Expected: 8× NVIDIA H100, PCIe Gen5

echo "=== STEP 2: Update Firmware (use NVIDIA Firmware Updater) ==="
# Download latest FW from NVIDIA Enterprise Support portal
# ./nvidia-firmware-updater --gpu --nvswitch --nic
# Reboot after firmware update

echo "=== STEP 3: Install GPU Operator (via Helm on K8s control plane) ==="
# The GPU Operator automatically installs:
# - NVIDIA GPU driver (matching H100 — 550.x or later)
# - NVIDIA Container Toolkit (nvidia-docker2 replacement)
# - NVIDIA K8s Device Plugin (nvidia.com/gpu resource)
# - DCGM Exporter (Prometheus GPU metrics on :9400)
# - GPU Feature Discovery (node labels: nvidia.com/gpu.product=H100)
# - MIG Manager (if MIG is configured)

echo "=== STEP 4: Verify GPU Operator Deployment ==="
kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator
# Expected: nvidia-driver-daemonset (1 per GPU node)
#           nvidia-container-toolkit-daemonset
#           nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset
#           nvidia-dcgm-exporter (Prometheus metrics)

echo "=== STEP 5: Validate GPU Accessibility ==="
kubectl run gpu-test --rm -it --restart=Never \
  --image=nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:12.4.0-runtime-ubuntu22.04 \
  --limits=nvidia.com/gpu=1 \
  -- nvidia-smi
# Should show 1× H100 available to the pod

echo "=== STEP 6: Run DCGM Diagnostics ==="
kubectl exec -it -n gpu-operator $(kubectl get pod -n gpu-operator -l app=nvidia-dcgm-exporter -o name | head -1) -- \
  dcgmi diag -r 3  # Level 3 = Full stress test (30+ min)
# All GPUs must pass all diagnostic tests

echo "✅ DGX node ${HOSTNAME} bootstrapped successfully"

⚠️ GPU Driver Updates — The SRE's Most Dangerous Task

GPU driver updates are the #1 cause of GPU cluster outages. Unlike CPU microcode, GPU drivers are complex kernel modules that can take down the entire node. Golden rules: (1) NEVER update drivers without a maintenance window. (2) ALWAYS test on a non-production DGX first. (3) Use the GPU Operator's automatic canary rollout — upgrade one node, validate for 24h, then proceed. (4) Have a rollback plan: keep the previous driver version available (nvidia-driver-${OLD_VERSION}). (5) Use NVIDIA's documented driver/firmware compatibility matrix — mismatched driver+fw = XID 119 (illegal instruction) errors. For anihpj: driver updates happen during the Sunday 02:00-06:00 maintenance window, one DGX at a time, with NCCL all-reduce validation after each node.

Stage 5: Decommission — Secure GPU Disposal

Decommissioning a DGX isn't just unracking it. GPUs contain HBM memory that could hold sensitive model weights or training data. Secure wipe procedure: (1) Run nvidia-smi --gpu-reset on all 8 GPUs (clears HBM). (2) Boot into NVIDIA's secure erase utility — performs a full HBM memory overwrite with random data. (3) Factory reset NVSwitch and BMC firmware to defaults. (4) Physically remove and shred any local NVMe drives. (5) Document GPU serial numbers for asset management and environmental compliance (GPUs are e-waste under WEEE directive).

31.3 Monitoring & Observability — The SRE's GPU Dashboard

Chapter 21 covered DCGM, Prometheus, and Grafana in detail. This section is the SRE's operational perspective — what you actually monitor day-to-day, the alerts that wake you up, and the dashboards you live in. Monitoring GPU infrastructure is fundamentally different from monitoring web services: you're tracking hardware health (XID errors, ECC, thermal) alongside software metrics (inference latency, training throughput).

The SRE's 5 Golden Signals — Adapted for GPU Infrastructure

Google SRE defines four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation). For GPU infrastructure, we add a fifth:

1️⃣ Latency

Inference: Triton P95 latency per model version. Alert if P95 >50ms (anihpj SLA). Training: Batch processing time. If batch-time increases → data pipeline bottleneck. GPU: Kernel execution time (from Nsight).

2️⃣ Throughput

Inference: Requests/second served by Triton. Must scale linearly with GPU count. Training: Samples/second processed. Declining throughput = NCCL degradation or thermal throttling. Data: GB/s from storage to GPU (GPUDirect Storage BW).

3️⃣ Errors

Hardware: XID errors (any non-zero = alarm), Double-bit ECC, GPU offline events. Software: CUDA errors, NCCL timeouts, Triton inference failures. Data: Corrupted checkpoints, failed data loads.

4️⃣ Saturation

GPU: Utilization >95% sustained = saturated. GPU memory >95% = OOM risk. NVLink: Bandwidth >85% of 900 GB/s. IB: Fabric congestion >70%. Power: GPU drawing near TDP limit (700W H100).

5️⃣ 🆕 Hardware Health

Thermal: GPU temp, memory temp, hotspot temp. Throttle threshold: 85°C. ECC: SB errors (correctable, >100/hr = degrading), DB errors (uncorrectable, any = P1). Power: PCIe + 8-pin power stability. Clock throttling reasons (thermal, power, utilization).

31.4 Incident Response & Troubleshooting — GPU Firefighting

GPU incidents are different from web service incidents. A crashed pod restarts in seconds. A GPU with double-bit ECC errors needs physical replacement — there is no kubectl delete pod fix. This section covers the six most common GPU incidents, their symptoms, diagnostic commands, and resolution procedures.

🔥 Incident #1: GPU Fell Off the Bus (XID 79)

😰 Symptoms
  • nvidia-smi shows only 7 GPUs instead of 8 on a DGX
  • dmesg | grep NVRM shows: "NVRM: GPU at PCI:0000:XX:00.0 has fallen off the bus"
  • DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL = -1 (GPU unreachable)
  • Any training job using that GPU hangs or crashes with CUDA error
🔍 Diagnosis (5 minutes)
  1. nvidia-smi — confirm GPU missing from list
  2. dmesg | grep -i nvrm | tail -20 — confirm XID 79
  3. lspci | grep NVIDIA — is GPU visible at PCI level?
  4. Try GPU reset: nvidia-smi -i <GPU_ID> --gpu-reset (only if GPU still partially visible)
  5. Check physical: any loose power cables? NVLink bridge seated?
✅ Resolution
  1. kubectl cordon <node> — stop scheduling new GPU workloads
  2. kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data — evict running pods
  3. Attempt nvidia-smi -i <GPU_ID> --gpu-reset — works ~30% of the time
  4. If reset fails → full node reboot → if GPU still missing → physical RMA required
  5. File NVIDIA support ticket with: DGX serial, GPU serial, dmesg output, DCGM diagnostic report
  6. Schedule GPU replacement (NBD advance replacement with NVAIE support contract)

MTTR target: 4 hours (with NVAIE NBD replacement). Prevention: DCGM XID monitoring catches this before GPU becomes completely unreachable.

🔥 Incident #2: NCCL Timeout / Hang During Distributed Training

😰 Symptoms
  • Training job hangs at a specific step — no progress for minutes
  • NCCL logs show: "NCCL WARN NET/IB : Got completion with error" or "NCCL INFO TIMEOUT"
  • One GPU shows 100% utilization, others at 0% — NCCL ring is broken
  • PyTorch DDP shows: "Process group timeout" after NCCL_BLOCKING_WAIT threshold
🔍 Diagnosis (5-10 minutes)
  1. Enable verbose NCCL logging: export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=ALL
  2. Check NVLink status: nvidia-smi nvlink -s -i 0 — any links inactive?
  3. Check InfiniBand: ibstat — are all 8 IB ports active? Link down on any?
  4. Check for NCCL_IB_DISABLE being accidentally set: echo $NCCL_IB_DISABLE
  5. Run NCCL bandwidth test: nccl-tests/build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 128M -f 2 -g 8
✅ Resolution
  1. Kill the hung training job: kubectl delete pod <training-pod> --force --grace-period=0
  2. Set NCCL timeout env vars before restarting: NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT=22, NCCL_IB_RETRY_CNT=7
  3. If IB link down: check physical cable → replace if needed → restart IB subnet manager
  4. If NVLink inactive: run nvidia-smi nvlink -r (reset NVLink) → if still inactive, schedule GPU re-seating
  5. Restart training from last checkpoint (MLflow should have the checkpoint path)

MTTR target: 30 minutes. Prevention: Pre-flight NCCL all-reduce test before every training job launch. Set NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT=22 to fail fast instead of hanging.

🔥 Incident #3: CUDA Out of Memory (OOM)

😰 Symptoms
  • Training/inference pod crashes with: "RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate X MiB"
  • nvidia-smi shows FB (framebuffer) usage at ~100% just before the crash
  • OOMKilled if Kubernetes memory limits are set
🔍 Diagnosis (2 minutes)
  1. kubectl logs <pod> | grep "out of memory" — confirm CUDA OOM
  2. Check current GPU memory allocation: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv
  3. What was the batch size? Model size? Any other processes on the GPU?
✅ Resolution
  1. Reduce batch size (try halving it — 256 → 128 → 64)
  2. Enable gradient checkpointing (trades compute for memory): model.gradient_checkpointing_enable()
  3. Use mixed precision (FP16 instead of FP32): torch.cuda.amp.autocast()
  4. Use MIG for multi-tenant isolation — a dev's leaky notebook won't OOM production inference
  5. For inference: Check Triton's max_batch_size — too large batches cause OOM. Use dynamic batching with a smaller max.

🔥 Incident #4: Thermal Throttling Cascade

😰 Symptoms
  • Training throughput (samples/sec) gradually declines over 30 minutes
  • GPU clock speeds dropping: nvidia-smi -q -d CLOCK shows SM clock below base
  • All GPUs in the rack showing elevated temperatures (82-88°C)
  • nvidia-smi shows "SW Thermal Slowdown" as Active
✅ Resolution
  1. Immediately reduce GPU workload intensity: lower batch size, pause non-critical jobs
  2. Check data center cooling: is the CDU (Coolant Distribution Unit) running? Supply temp within spec?
  3. Check for blocked airflow: clogged filters, blocked cold aisle, adjacent equipment exhausting hot air
  4. Verify liquid cooling loop: pump speed, flow rate, no air in the loop
  5. If persistent: schedule emergency cooling maintenance. GPUs running at >85°C for extended periods have reduced lifespan.

MTTR target: 1 hour for temporary mitigation, 4 hours for root cause fix.

31.5 Cost Optimization & Capacity Planning — GPU FinOps

GPU infrastructure is expensive — a single idle H100 costs ~$12/hour in the cloud, and a DGX H100 depreciates at ~$8/hour over its 3-year life. GPU FinOps (Financial Operations) is the discipline of maximizing ROI from every GPU dollar. This section covers the strategies, tools, and metrics you need to run cost-efficient GPU infrastructure.

💰 Strategy 1: Spot/Preemptible GPU Instances — Save 60-90%

Cloud providers offer unused GPU capacity at massive discounts — but with the risk of termination on 2-minute notice. For fault-tolerant training jobs, this is pure savings.

Python — anihpj Spot GPU Training with Checkpoint/Resume
# anihpj Spot GPU Training with Graceful Preemption Handling
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import signal
import os

CHECKPOINT_PATH = "/checkpoints/anihpj_job_rec_latest.pt"

def save_checkpoint(model, optimizer, epoch, step, loss):
    """Save checkpoint to resilient storage (S3/WEKA/NFS — NOT local NVMe)"""
    torch.save({
        'epoch': epoch, 'step': step,
        'model_state_dict': model.state_dict(),
        'optimizer_state_dict': optimizer.state_dict(),
        'loss': loss,
        'random_state': torch.get_rng_state()  # For reproducibility
    }, CHECKPOINT_PATH)
    # Also upload to S3 for cross-AZ resilience
    os.system(f"aws s3 cp {CHECKPOINT_PATH} s3://anihpj-checkpoints/")

def handle_preemption(signum, frame):
    """AWS Spot Instance sends SIGTERM 2 minutes before termination"""
    print("⚠️ Spot preemption signal received! Saving checkpoint...")
    save_checkpoint(model, optimizer, current_epoch, current_step, current_loss)
    if dist.is_initialized():
        dist.barrier()  # Wait for all ranks to save
    print("✅ Checkpoint saved. Exiting gracefully.")
    exit(0)

# Register preemption handler
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handle_preemption)

# Training loop — resumes automatically on new spot instance
if os.path.exists(CHECKPOINT_PATH):
    checkpoint = torch.load(CHECKPOINT_PATH)
    model.load_state_dict(checkpoint['model_state_dict'])
    optimizer.load_state_dict(checkpoint['optimizer_state_dict'])
    start_epoch = checkpoint['epoch']
    print(f"🔄 Resumed from epoch {start_epoch}, step {checkpoint['step']}")
else:
    start_epoch = 0
    print("🆕 Starting fresh training run")

# Cost comparison for anihpj 8-GPU training (4 hours):
# On-Demand H100: 8 × $12/hr × 4h = $384/run
# Spot H100:      8 × $3/hr  × 4h = $96/run  (75% savings!)
# With 1 preemption/run (adds ~15 min): $96 → $108 (72% savings)

💰 Strategy 3: Idle GPU Detection & Auto-Shutdown

The #1 source of GPU waste is idle GPUs — a data scientist launches a Jupyter notebook, goes to lunch, and the GPU sits idle at $12/hr for two hours. Auto-shutdown policies eliminate this waste.

Prometheus Alert — Auto-Shutdown Idle Dev GPUs
# Prometheus rule for idle GPU detection
groups:
- name: gpu-cost-optimization
  rules:
  - alert: GPUIdleDev
    expr: |
      DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL{env="dev"} < 10
      and
      DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED{env="dev"} / DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_TOTAL{env="dev"} < 0.1
    for: 30m
    labels:
      severity: info
      cost_impact: "high"  # ~$6 wasted per 30min idle
    annotations:
      summary: "Dev GPU {{ $labels.gpu }} idle for 30+ minutes"
      description: "{{ $labels.user }}'s GPU is idle. Auto-scaling down."
      action: "kubectl scale deployment {{ $labels.deployment }} --replicas=0"

# Auto-remediation: Webhook receiver calls anihpj GPU scaler
# POST to https://gpu-scaler.anihpj.internal/scale-down
# Body: {"gpu": "{{ $labels.gpu }}", "user": "{{ $labels.user }}", "reason": "idle_30min"}

📊 GPU Cost Allocation — Chargeback by Team/Project

SQL — GPU Cost Allocation Query (anihpj FinOps Dashboard)
-- GPU cost allocation by team for monthly invoice
SELECT
    team,
    SUM(gpu_hours) AS total_gpu_hours,
    SUM(gpu_hours * CASE
        WHEN gpu_type = 'H100' THEN 12.00   -- On-demand cloud pricing
        WHEN gpu_type = 'A100' THEN 4.00
        WHEN gpu_type = 'L40S' THEN 2.00
        WHEN gpu_type = 'T4'   THEN 0.40
    END) AS estimated_cost_usd,
    AVG(gpu_utilization) AS avg_gpu_util_pct,
    -- Efficiency score: high util = good, low util = wasting money
    CASE
        WHEN AVG(gpu_utilization) > 80 THEN '🟢 Efficient'
        WHEN AVG(gpu_utilization) > 50 THEN '🟡 Needs Review'
        ELSE '🔴 Wasting Money'
    END AS efficiency_rating
FROM gpu_usage_metrics
WHERE month = DATE_TRUNC('month', CURRENT_DATE)
GROUP BY team
ORDER BY estimated_cost_usd DESC;

💡 SRE Insight: The GPU Efficiency Scorecard

Create a monthly GPU efficiency scorecard per team. The formula: Efficiency = (GPU-hours with util >80%) / (Total GPU-hours allocated). Teams with efficiency <50% get their GPU quota reduced next month. This gamification alone reduced anihpj's GPU waste by 35% in the first quarter.

31.6 Security & Compliance — Hardening GPU Infrastructure

GPU infrastructure introduces unique security challenges: GPU memory can contain sensitive model weights, NGC containers come from external registries, and MIG isolation must be verified at the hardware level. This section covers the security controls every NVIDIA SRE must implement.

🔒 NGC Container Scanning

Threat: Pre-built containers from NGC may contain vulnerabilities. Control: Mirror NGC images to a private registry (Harbor/ECR). Scan every image with Trivy/Grype before allowing deployment. Only allow images from anihpj-registry.internal/ in K8s admission policies. Update base images within 7 days of NVIDIA CVE patches.

🔒 MIG Tenant Isolation

Threat: One MIG tenant accessing another's GPU memory. Control: MIG provides hardware-level isolation (separate memory channels, separate L2 cache slices, separate SM groups). Verify with NVIDIA's MIG validation suite: nvidia-smi mig -i 0 --verify. Never use MIG for tenants with different security classifications (PCI vs HIPAA).

🔒 GPU BMC/IPMI Hardening

Threat: BMC (Baseboard Management Controller) on DGX provides out-of-band access — if compromised, attacker has physical-level GPU control. Control: Put BMC on isolated management VLAN. Use strong, rotated passwords. Enable BMC audit logging. Never expose BMC to the internet. Disable IPMI over LAN if not needed.

🔒 Secure Boot + Firmware Attestation

Threat: Compromised GPU firmware. Control: Enable Secure Boot on DGX. Verify GPU firmware signatures before loading. Use NVIDIA's Firmware Attestation to cryptographically verify GPU firmware hasn't been tampered with. Integrate attestation into node bootstrap — a GPU that fails attestation is automatically cordoned.

🔒 K8s NetworkPolicy for GPU Pods

Threat: GPU training pods communicating with untrusted endpoints (data exfiltration). Control: Default-deny NetworkPolicy. Only allow egress to MLflow, S3 checkpoint bucket, and container registry. Block all other egress from GPU pods. Use egressgateway for controlled outbound access.

🔒 Secrets Management

Threat: NGC API keys, S3 credentials hardcoded in containers. Control: Use K8s Secrets + External Secrets Operator (AWS Secrets Manager/Vault). Never bake credentials into container images. Rotate NGC API keys quarterly. Use IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) for S3 access instead of static credentials.

⚠️ GPU Security Gotcha — CUDA IPC and Cross-Pod Memory Access

CUDA Inter-Process Communication (IPC) allows GPU memory sharing between processes. If two K8s pods run on the same GPU (time-slicing or MIG misconfiguration), CUDA IPC could theoretically enable cross-pod memory access. Mitigation: Always use MIG for multi-tenant GPU sharing (hardware isolation). Never use GPU time-slicing for tenants with different trust levels. Verify MIG configuration: nvidia-smi mig -i 0 --display shows which compute instances own which memory slices.

31.7 Automation & IaC for GPU Infrastructure

Manual GPU management is unsustainable at any scale beyond 2 nodes. Every GPU operation — provisioning, driver updates, health checks, node cordon/drain — must be automated. This section covers the IaC patterns and automation tools for GPU infrastructure.

🏗️ Infrastructure as Code — Three-Layer GPU Automation

☸️
Layer 3: Kubernetes (GitOps)

ArgoCD / Flux sync GPU workloads from Git. TrainingJob, InferenceDeployment, MIGPartition — all declarative YAML in Git. Drift detection auto-remediates. Tools: ArgoCD, Flux, Kustomize, Helm.

🏗️
Layer 2: Configuration Management (Ansible)

Ansible playbooks for GPU driver/firmware updates, DCGM configuration, IB fabric validation, /etc/docker/daemon.json GPU settings. Triggered by CI/CD pipeline, not manual SSH. Tools: Ansible, Packer (immutable GPU node images).

🖥️
Layer 1: Infrastructure Provisioning (Terraform)

Terraform provisions cloud GPU instances (AWS p5, Azure ND, GCP a3), on-prem DGX via Redfish API, InfiniBand switch configuration, and VLAN/network setup. Tools: Terraform, OpenTofu, Crossplane.

🔄 Automated GPU Node Lifecycle with Ansible

Ansible — GPU Node Maintenance Playbook
# anihpj-gpu-maintenance.yaml
# Run: ansible-playbook -i inventory/gpu-nodes gpu-maintenance.yaml
- name: GPU Node Maintenance
  hosts: gpu_nodes
  become: yes
  vars:
    maintenance_mode: "{{ maintenance_mode | default('drain') }}"
    new_driver_version: "550.90.07"
    
  tasks:
    - name: Pre-flight — Run DCGM diagnostic
      shell: dcgmi diag -r 1  # Quick 2-min health check
      register: dcgm_result
      
    - name: Abort if DCGM fails
      fail:
        msg: "DCGM diag failed on {{ inventory_hostname }}"
      when: "'FAIL' in dcgm_result.stdout"

    - name: Cordon node in Kubernetes
      shell: kubectl cordon {{ inventory_hostname }}
      when: maintenance_mode == 'drain'
      
    - name: Drain GPU workloads
      shell: kubectl drain {{ inventory_hostname }} --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=300s
      when: maintenance_mode == 'drain'

    - name: Update NVIDIA GPU driver
      apt:
        name: "nvidia-driver-{{ new_driver_version }}"
        state: latest
      notify: Reboot node

    - name: Update GPU firmware (if available)
      shell: |
        /opt/nvidia/firmware-updater/nvidia-fw-updater \
          --gpu --nvswitch --nic --auto-reboot=no
      when: firmware_update is defined and firmware_update

    - name: Verify GPU health post-update
      shell: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version,serial --format=csv
      register: gpu_check

    - name: Uncordon node
      shell: kubectl uncordon {{ inventory_hostname }}
      when: maintenance_mode == 'drain'
🏆 The anihpj GPU Automation Maturity Model

Level 1 — Manual (Startup): SSH into each GPU node. Run nvidia-smi manually. kubectl cordon/drain by hand. Driver updates via apt-get. Time per operation: 30 minutes.

Level 2 — Scripted (Growing): Bash scripts for common tasks. Ansible playbooks for driver updates. Time per operation: 10 minutes.

Level 3 — Automated (Mature): GPU Operator handles driver/toolkit. ArgoCD syncs GPU workloads. Auto-remediation for node failures. DCGM triggers auto-cordon. Time per operation: 30 seconds (review and approve).

Level 4 — Self-Healing (World-Class): ML-driven anomaly detection triggers preemptive GPU migration before hardware failure. Spot instance interruption handled automatically with checkpoint/resume. Capacity auto-scales based on job queue depth. Time per operation: 0 seconds (fully automated).

anihpj target: Level 3 within 6 months of GPU cluster deployment. Level 4 within 18 months.

Q1

What are the five golden signals for GPU infrastructure monitoring, and which NVIDIA tool provides the data for each?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Latency (Triton P95, DCGM kernel times), Throughput (samples/sec from MLflow, req/sec from Triton), Errors (XID errors, CUDA errors from DCGM), Saturation (GPU-Util %, FB-Used %, NVLink BW % from DCGM), and Hardware Health (GPU temp, ECC errors, power draw from DCGM). DCGM is the primary data source for all five; Prometheus scrapes DCGM metrics; Grafana visualizes them.

  ──────────────────────────           ─────────────────────────────
  Latency:    Request duration          Latency:   Triton P95, kernel exec time
  Traffic:    Requests/sec              Throughput: Samples/sec, req/sec, GB/s
  Errors:     HTTP 5xx rate             Errors:    XID codes, CUDA errors, DBE ECC
  Saturation: CPU/Mem usage             Saturation: GPU-Util%, FB-Used%, NVLink BW%
                                        🆕 Hardware Health: GPU Temp, ECC trend, Power

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GPU (H100) ──DCGM──▶ Prometheus ──▶ Grafana ──▶ PagerDuty/Slack        │
  │  │                      │              │              │                  │
  │  │ 50+ metrics/sec      │ scrapes/15s  │ dashboards   │ P1=wake, P2=push│

The five golden signals are adapted from Google's SRE book because GPU infrastructure has unique failure modes (hardware degradation, thermal throttling, ECC errors) that web services don't experience. DCGM exports ALL five categories of metrics to Prometheus. The SRE configures Prometheus alerting rules with severity-based routing (P1→PagerDuty phone call, P2→Slack notification, P3→Jira ticket) based on thresholds defined in Ch 21.

Q2

You receive a P1 alert: "XID 79 on DGX-02 GPU-3." What are your first five actions, and what is the target MTTR?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

1. Acknowledge alert (30s) — stops escalation. 2. Verify with nvidia-smi and dmesg | grep NVRM. 3. Cordon + drain the node (kubectl cordon + kubectl drain). 4. Attempt GPU reset: nvidia-smi -i 3 --gpu-reset. 5. If reset fails, reboot node; if GPU still missing, file RMA. Target MTTR: 4 hours with NVAIE NBD replacement. Auto-remediation should cordon the GPU before you even acknowledge the alert.

💡 EXPLANATION — XID 79 Incident Response Flow
  XID 79 = "GPU has fallen off the bus" — The GPU electrically disconnected from PCIe
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    XID 79 INCIDENT RESPONSE — 5 MINUTE FLOW               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⏱️ T+0:00  PagerDuty ALERT: XID 79, DGX-02, GPU-3                      │
  │  ⏱️ T+0:30  ACKNOWLEDGE → stops escalation chain (manager NOT called)    │
  │  ⏱️ T+1:00  VERIFY: ssh dgx-02 → nvidia-smi → 7 GPUs not 8 ❌           │
  │            dmesg | grep NVRM → "GPU at PCI:0000:XX has fallen off bus"   │
  │  ⏱️ T+2:00  CORDON: kubectl cordon dgx-02 (stop new GPU pods)           │
  │            DRAIN:  kubectl drain dgx-02 --ignore-daemonsets              │
  │  ⏱️ T+3:00  RESET ATTEMPT: nvidia-smi -i 3 --gpu-reset                  │
  │            ├─ Works (30% chance) → GPU reappears → rejoins cluster       │
  │            └─ Fails (70% chance) → proceed to reboot                     │
  │  ⏱️ T+4:00  REBOOT: shutdown -r now dgx-02                              │
  │            ├─ POST reboot → GPU reappears → reseat suspected             │
  │            └─ GPU still missing → HARDWARE FAILURE → RMA                 │
  │  ⏱️ T+5:00  FILE RMA: nvidia-bug-report.sh output + XID code + GPU S/N  │
  │            MTTR TARGET: <4 hours with NVAIE NBD advance replacement      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  🔑 KEY: Auto-remediation (DCGM→GPU Operator) cordons the GPU in <30s —
  before you even wake up. Your job is verification + escalation + RMA.

XID 79 is one of the most serious GPU errors because it means the GPU has electrically disconnected from the PCIe bus — it's as if you physically pulled the GPU out while the server was running. Common causes: power delivery issues (bad PSU/VRM), PCIe riser problems, or GPU hardware failure. The auto-remediation system (DCGM detects GPU-Util=-1 → GPU Operator cordons node) should fire within 30 seconds — before the SRE even acknowledges the PagerDuty alert. Your manual steps focus on verification, recovery attempts, and RMA filing if recovery fails.

Q3

What is the most dangerous routine task for a GPU SRE, and what five safeguards should be in place?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU driver updates are the #1 cause of GPU cluster outages. Safeguards: (1) Always use a maintenance window — never update during production hours. (2) Test on a non-production DGX first for 24h. (3) Use GPU Operator's canary rollout — update one node at a time. (4) Have a rollback plan with the previous driver version available. (5) Verify driver/firmware compatibility matrix — mismatched versions cause XID 119 (illegal instruction) errors.

💡 EXPLANATION — The GPU Driver Update Minefield
  GPU DRIVER UPDATES — Why This Is the #1 Cause of Outages
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │  THE DANGER: GPU drivers are KERNEL MODULES. A buggy driver can:         │
  │  • Panic the entire node (not just one GPU)                              │
  │  • Cause XID 119 (illegal instruction) if driver+fw mismatch            │
  │  • Change clock/power policies → silent 40% perf regression              │
  │  • Reset MIG configurations → tenants can see each other's GPUs          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  THE 5 SAFEGUARDS — CANARY ROLLOUT STRATEGY:                             │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ DAY 1:  Test on 1 CANARY node (non-production DGX)              │    │
  │  │         • Run DCGM diag -r 3 (30 min stress)                    │    │
  │  │         • Run NCCL all-reduce benchmark (verify 400+ GB/s)       │    │
  │  │         • Run representative training job for 24h                │    │
  │  │         • ✅ All tests pass → proceed to Stage 2                 │    │
  │  │ DAY 2:  Rollout to 10% of fleet (2 nodes in 20-node cluster)    │    │
  │  │         • Monitor for 24h: GPU-Util, Temp, XID, ECC, throughput │    │
  │  │ DAY 3:  Rollout to 50% of fleet                                 │    │
  │  │ DAY 4:  Rollout to 100% of fleet                                │    │
  │  │ ROLLBACK PLAN (at any stage):                                   │    │
  │  │   helm rollback gpu-operator → reverts driver DaemonSet          │    │
  │  │   OR: apt install nvidia-driver-${OLD_VERSION} on bare metal    │    │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Unlike a web server package update (which at worst restarts a service), a GPU driver update is a kernel module reload — it affects every process using the GPU, including running training jobs worth thousands of dollars. The canary strategy isolates blast radius. If the canary node shows ANY regression (XID errors, clock drops, NCCL BW reduction), the rollout is halted. The GPU Operator (Ch 10) automates this canary rollout on Kubernetes — you configure the update strategy in Helm values and the Operator handles node-by-node drain, update, validation, and uncordon.

Q4

How does MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) help with GPU cost optimization? Give a concrete savings example.

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

MIG splits one physical A100/H100 into up to 7 isolated GPU instances with dedicated compute, memory, and L2 cache. Example: Before MIG — 4 separate GPUs for dev, staging, QA, and CI/CD at $12/hr each = $48/hr total. After MIG — 1 A100 split into 4 MIG slices (2×20GB + 2×10GB) at $4/hr spot = 91% cost reduction. MIG also provides hardware-level isolation, preventing noisy-neighbor problems that plague GPU time-slicing or vGPU.

💡 EXPLANATION — MIG Hardware Partitioning vs Software Time-Slicing
  MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) — Hardware-Level GPU Partitioning
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │  1× A100 80GB GPU → 7 ISOLATED INSTANCES (Hardware Partitioning)        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  MIG PROFILES: 7g.80gb | 4g.40gb | 3g.40gb | 2g.20gb | 1g.10gb│   │
  │  │  ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬──────┬──────┐│   │
  │  │  │ 3g.40gb │ 2g.20gb │ 1g.10gb │ 1g.10gb │ 1g.10gb │1g.5gb│1g.5gb││   │
  │  │  │ 42 SMs  │ 28 SMs  │ 14 SMs  │ 14 SMs  │ 14 SMs  │ 7 SMs│ 7 SMs││   │
  │  │  │ 40 GB   │ 20 GB   │ 10 GB   │ 10 GB   │ 10 GB   │ 5 GB │ 5 GB ││   │
  │  │  │ 🏋️ Train│ 🚀 Stag │ 🔧 Dev  │ 🧪 QA   │ 🛠️ CI/CD│ 📓 DS │ 📓 DS ││   │
  │  │  └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴──────┴──────┘│   │
  │  │  ✅ EACH slice gets: OWN memory channels, OWN L2 cache, OWN SMs   │   │
  │  │  ✅ Fault isolation: GPU OOM in Dev slice CANNOT affect Training   │   │
  │  │  ✅ QoS guaranteed: Each slice gets its allocated BW, not best-effort│  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  MIG (HARDWARE)              vs          GPU TIME-SLICING (SOFTWARE)     │
  │  ─────────────────────                   ──────────────────────────      │
  │  ✅ Dedicated memory channels             ❌ Shared memory pool           │
  │  ✅ Dedicated L2 cache slices             ❌ Shared L2 (cache thrashing)  │
  │  ✅ Dedicated SM groups                   ❌ Context-switch overhead      │
  │  ✅ Fault isolation (OOM stays local)     ❌ OOM kills all tenants        │
  │  ✅ Predictable latency                   ❌ Jitter from other workloads  │
  │  ✅ Max 7 instances per GPU               ❌ Unlimited (but slow)         │
  │  💰 COST: Before = 4 GPUs × $12/hr = $48/hr → After = 1 GPU × $4 = $4/hr│
  │     SAVINGS: 91% for non-production workloads                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MIG is NVIDIA's answer to GPU multi-tenancy. Unlike vGPU (software-level, best-effort sharing) or time-slicing (context switching), MIG physically partitions the GPU at the hardware level. Each MIG instance gets its own dedicated memory channels, L2 cache slices, and SM groups — providing guaranteed QoS and fault isolation. For anihpj's non-production environments (dev, staging, QA, CI/CD), MIG enables 7 teams to share 1 A100 with the same isolation as having 7 separate GPUs — at 1/7th the cost. NCA-AIIO exam note: MIG works on A100 and H100 only. Max 7 instances. vGPU requires NVAIE license; MIG does not (it's a hardware feature).

Q5

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Level 1 (Manual): SSH into nodes, run nvidia-smi manually, cordon/drain by hand. 30 min/op. Level 2 (Scripted): Bash scripts + Ansible. 10 min/op. Level 3 (Automated): GPU Operator handles drivers, ArgoCD syncs workloads, DCGM auto-cordons on failure, auto-remediation for node failures. 30 sec/op. Level 4 (Self-Healing): ML-driven anomaly detection preemptively migrates workloads before hardware failure. 0 sec/op. anihpj target: Level 3 within 6 months.

The jump from Level 2 to Level 3 is the hardest — it requires adopting GitOps, building auto-remediation pipelines, and trusting automation. Level 4 is aspirational for most teams; only hyperscalers (Google, Meta, OpenAI) operate at this level. anihpj's realistic target: Level 3 within 6 months of GPU cluster deployment. The GPU Operator (Ch 10) is the single most important tool for reaching Level 3.

Q6

What security controls are specific to GPU infrastructure that a traditional Linux SRE might overlook?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Five GPU-specific security controls: (1) NGC container scanning — mirror to private registry, scan with Trivy, only allow private registry images. (2) MIG isolation verification — MIG provides hardware-level isolation but must be verified; never use time-slicing for different trust levels. (3) BMC/IPMI hardening — DGX BMC provides out-of-band GPU control; isolate on management VLAN, never expose to internet. (4) CUDA IPC risks — inter-process GPU memory sharing could enable cross-pod access if MIG is misconfigured. (5) GPU secure wipe — HBM memory retains data; must be securely erased before decommissioning with NVIDIA's secure erase utility.

💡 EXPLANATION — GPU-Specific Security Attack Surface
  GPU INFRASTRUCTURE — THE 5 SECURITY CONTROLS A LINUX SRE MIGHT MISS
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │  1️⃣ NGC CONTAINER SUPPLY CHAIN                                          │
  │  NGC (nvcr.io) ──▶ Private Registry (Harbor/ECR) ──▶ K8s Admission      │
  │  Public image      Trivy scan → CVE report   Only allow:                 │
  │  (untrusted)       Sign with Cosign          anihpj-registry.internal     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  2️⃣ MIG ISOLATION vs TIME-SLICING                                       │
  │  MIG (HARDWARE):  Dedicated mem + L2 + SMs → ✅ Multi-tenant safe        │
  │  Time-slicing:    Shared memory pool → ❌ Cross-tenant data leak          │
  │  🚨 NEVER use time-slicing for tenants with different trust levels        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  3️⃣ BMC/IPMI — THE BACKDOOR TO YOUR GPU                                 │
  │  BMC can: Power cycle GPUs, reflash firmware, access GPU console         │
  │  IF COMPROMISED: Attacker has PHYSICAL-LEVEL GPU control                 │
  │  DEFENSE: Isolated VLAN · Strong rotated passwords · Audit logging       │
  │           NEVER expose BMC to internet · Disable IPMI over LAN           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  4️⃣ CUDA IPC — Cross-Process GPU Memory Access                          │
  │  CUDA IPC allows GPU memory sharing between processes.                   │
  │  RISK: Pod A could read Pod B's GPU memory if sharing same GPU.          │
  │  MITIGATION: Always use MIG for multi-tenant GPU sharing.                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  5️⃣ GPU DECOMMISSIONING — Secure Wipe                                   │
  │  HBM memory RETAINS DATA after power-off (like RAM, but longer).         │
  │  WIPE: nvidia-smi --gpu-reset → NVIDIA Secure Erase → Factory reset     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A traditional Linux SRE secures the OS, network, and application layers. GPU infrastructure introduces entirely new attack surfaces: the BMC (out-of-band management that can reflash firmware), CUDA IPC (inter-process GPU memory sharing), container supply chain (NGC images from external registry), and HBM memory persistence (data survives power-off). These are NOT covered by standard Linux hardening guides — they require GPU-specific security knowledge that this guide teaches in Chapters 6, 10, 29, and 31.

Q7

Describe the GPU cluster lifecycle from provisioning to decommissioning. What are the key validation steps at each stage?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Provision: Verify 3-phase 415V power + liquid cooling BEFORE unboxing. Run DCGM diag -r 3 for acceptance testing — reject any GPU that fails. Bootstrap: GPU Operator auto-installs drivers + toolkit. Validate with nvidia-smi and NCCL bandwidth test. Operate: Daily health checks, monthly deep diagnostics, quarterly driver updates. Maintain: Monthly maintenance windows for firmware, NVLink re-seating, cooling service. Decommission: GPU secure wipe (HBM overwrite), factory reset NVSwitch/BMC, shred NVMe drives, document serial numbers for e-waste compliance.

The GPU cluster lifecycle spans 3-5 years from unboxing to decommission. The most expensive mistake is skipping Stage 1 validation — accepting a DGX that hasn't passed DCGM Level 3 diagnostics means you'll discover the faulty GPU during a production training run, wasting thousands in compute time. The second most expensive mistake is neglecting Stage 4 maintenance — NVLink links degrade over time, and without periodic re-seating, training throughput silently drops 20-40%.

Q8

What is the difference between a traditional SRE and an NVIDIA SRE? Why does CUDA knowledge matter for troubleshooting?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

A traditional SRE seeing "GPU-Util 100% but training slow" would be stuck. An NVIDIA SRE knows to check: (1) Are Tensor Cores being used or just CUDA cores? (ncu --set full), (2) Is the kernel memory-bound? (SM efficiency vs memory throughput), (3) Is NCCL using NVLink or falling back to PCIe? (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO), (4) Are there bank conflicts? (ncu --section MemoryWorkloadAnalysis). This depth — understanding that GPU-Util % can be misleading — is what separates a GPU SRE from a generic SRE. NVIDIA SRE/PE roles command 20-40% higher compensation because this skill stack is deeper and rarer.

💡 EXPLANATION — Why GPU-Util % Is Misleading
  THE GPU-UTIL TRAP — Why 100% Doesn't Mean Fast
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  nvidia-smi GPU-Util measures: "Was ANY compute pipeline active?"        │
  │  It does NOT measure: "Was it doing USEFUL work efficiently?"            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SCENARIO: Training dropped from 42K samples/sec to 25K (-40%)          │
  │  nvidia-smi: GPU-Util = 92% (looks fine!)                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  TRADITIONAL SRE: "GPU is busy. Must be a code issue."                  │
  │  → Wrong! Spends 2 hours debugging PyTorch code.                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  NVIDIA SRE (Your Approach):                                             │
  │  ✅ ncu --set full → SM Efficiency = 38% (should be >60%)                │
  │     → GPU stalls 62% of cycles waiting on memory                         │
  │  ✅ nvidia-smi nvlink -s → Link 3 at 120 GB/s (should be 900!)          │
  │     → Degraded NVLink slowing NCCL ring 7.5×                             │
  │  ✅ Root cause found in 5 minutes. Schedule GPU re-seating.              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  THE NVIDIA SRE TOOLKIT — Beyond nvidia-smi:                             │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ TOOL              WHAT IT REVEALS                   CHAPTER      │    │
  │  │ ────────────────  ────────────────────────────────  ───────────  │    │
  │  │ Nsight Compute    SM efficiency, mem BW, stalls     Ch 8, App C  │    │
  │  │ Nsight Systems    Timeline: CPU↔GPU, kernel overlap Ch 8, App C  │    │
  │  │ NCCL_DEBUG=INFO   NVLink vs PCIe path, topology      Ch 23       │    │
  │  │ DCGM metrics      FB-Used, NVLink-BW, XID errors     Ch 21       │    │
  │  │ nvidia-smi topo   GPU-PCIe-NUMA topology             Ch 21       │    │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💰 COMPENSATION: Traditional SRE $90-130K → NVIDIA SRE $130-180K       │
  │  The 20-40% premium is for this exact diagnostic depth.                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

GPU-Util % is the most misleading metric in GPU monitoring. It reports whether the compute pipeline was active — NOT whether it was doing efficient work. A GPU stalled on memory (scoreboard stall) still shows 100% utilization. NVIDIA SREs use Nsight Compute for kernel-level analysis — SM efficiency is the real metric. Traditional SREs don't learn these tools; NVIDIA SREs live in them daily. This is why the role commands a premium.

Q9

How would you set up a daily 5-minute GPU health check routine? What specific dashboards and commands would you use?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Minute 1: Grafana "GPU Overview" dashboard — scan all 32 GPUs for red/missing. Minute 2: XID Errors panel — any non-zero? GPU Temp heatmap — any >80°C? Minute 3: Training throughput trend — stable or declining? PagerDuty — any overnight incidents? Minute 4: Cost dashboard — any unexpected GPU spend spike? Minute 5: Quick SSH spot-check: nvidia-smi on one random DGX to verify Grafana matches reality. This 5-minute routine catches 90% of issues before they become P1/P2 incidents. The key principle: trust but verify — dashboards can lag or misreport.

The 5-minute routine is designed around signal-to-noise ratio. You don't deep-dive into every metric — you scan for red flags and anomalies. The spot-check (Minute 5) is critical: monitoring systems can lag or misreport, and the only way to be sure is to run a command directly on a GPU node. After this routine, you're ready for standup with a complete picture of cluster health.

Q10

A training job that normally takes 4 hours on 8 GPUs just took 7 hours. GPU utilization was reported at 92% throughout. What would you investigate?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU-Util at 92% means the GPU was busy — but not necessarily doing useful work efficiently. Investigate in order: (1) Thermal throttling: nvidia-smi -q -d CLOCK — did GPU clock speeds drop? (2) NVLink degradation: nvidia-smi nvlink -s — are all links at 900 GB/s? One degraded link slows the entire NCCL ring. (3) ECC errors: nvidia-smi -q -d ECC — any single-bit errors causing retries? (4) NCCL fallback to PCIe: Check NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs — did NCCL use NVLink or fall back to slow PCIe? (5) Data pipeline stall: Check batch loading time in MLflow — if GPU-Util oscillated 100%→0%→100%, the data pipeline is the bottleneck despite high average utilization. The key lesson: GPU-Util % alone is insufficient — you need SM efficiency, memory throughput, and NCCL bandwidth metrics to truly understand GPU performance.

💡 EXPLANATION — The 4hr→7hr Mystery: GPU-Util Deception
  CASE STUDY: Training 4hr → 7hr — Same Model, Same Data, Same GPU-Util 92%
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                          │
  │  THE SYMPTOM:                                                            │
  │  Training time: 4 hours (normal) → 7 hours (today) = 75% slower          │
  │  GPU-Util: 92% throughout — looks normal to a traditional SRE            │
  │  nvidia-smi: All 8 GPUs visible, no XID errors, no DBE ECC               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  THE DIAGNOSIS — Your 5-Step Investigation:                              │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ STEP 1: THERMAL CHECK                                            │    │
  │  │ nvidia-smi -q -d CLOCK → SM Clock: 1095 MHz (base: 1590 MHz)    │    │
  │  │ ▶ VERDICT: THERMAL THROTTLING! GPU clocks down 31%!              │    │
  │  │ ▶ FIX: Check CDU coolant temp. Clean dust filters.               │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │ STEP 2: NVLINK CHECK (if thermal was fine)                       │    │
  │  │ nvidia-smi nvlink -s → Link 3: 120 GB/s (should be 900 GB/s)    │    │
  │  │ ▶ NCCL ring bottlenecked on slow link. All other GPUs wait.      │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │ STEP 3: ECC CHECK (if NVLink was fine)                           │    │
  │  │ nvidia-smi -q -d ECC → GPU 3: 847 SB errors (72h cumulative)    │    │
  │  │ ▶ Memory retries adding latency. Schedule preventive RMA.        │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │ STEP 4: NCCL PATH CHECK                                          │    │
  │  │ NCCL_DEBUG=INFO → "Connected all rings, using NIC 0"             │    │
  │  │ ▶ NCCL using PCIe (64 GB/s) instead of NVLink (900 GB/s)!        │    │
  │  │ ▶ Check NCCL_IB_DISABLE env var.                                 │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │ STEP 5: DATA PIPELINE CHECK                                      │    │
  │  │ MLflow: batch_time=450ms, compute_time=120ms → 330ms data stall  │    │
  │  │ ▶ GPU spends 73% of time waiting for data, not computing!        │    │
  │  │ ▶ GPU-Util shows 92% because GPU IS active... just waiting.      │    │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🎯 KEY LESSON: GPU-Util % is the most dangerous metric in GPU ops      │
  │  because it creates a FALSE SENSE OF SECURITY. Always triangulate        │
  │  with SM efficiency, memory BW, NVLink BW, and batch timeline.           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is the classic "GPU-Util deception" scenario. The GPU was indeed busy — but busy WAITING, not computing. In the thermal throttling case (Step 1), the GPU clock dropped 31%, meaning every operation takes 31% longer, directly explaining the 4hr→7hr increase. But nvidia-smi still reports 92% utilization because the compute pipeline IS active — just at a slower clock. This is why the exam and real-world SRE work requires going beyond nvidia-smi. The investigation flow follows a priority order: thermal (most common) → NVLink (2nd most common) → ECC (degradation) → NCCL config (misconfiguration) → data pipeline (systemic).

🕐 09:03 — Spot-Check Verification (5 minutes)

Bash — SRE Monday Morning Spot-Check Script
#!/bin/bash
# monday-check.sh — Quick GPU cluster health verification

echo "=== 1. Verify all GPUs visible ==="
kubectl get nodes -l nvidia.com/gpu.product=H100 -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GPU:.status.capacity.nvidia\.com/gpu
# Expected: 4 nodes × 8 GPUs = 32 total

echo "=== 2. Random spot-check: DGX-01 GPU temp ==="
ssh dgx-01 "nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,temperature.gpu --format=csv,noheader"
# Expected: All <85°C. Investigate any >80°C

echo "=== 3. Check for XID errors overnight ==="
kubectl logs -n gpu-operator -l app=nvidia-dcgm-exporter --tail=100 | grep "xid"
# Expected: No output. Any output = investigate immediately.

echo "=== 4. Verify Triton is serving ==="
curl -s http://triton-inference.anihpj.svc:8000/v2/health/ready
# Expected: {"status":"ready"}

echo "=== 5. Check last training job ==="

# Verify: Status = Succeeded. Check MLflow for metrics.

echo "=== 6. Quick NCCL bandwidth test ==="

  --image=nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:24.02-py3 \
  --limits=nvidia.com/gpu=8 \
  -- /workspace/nccl-tests/build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 128M -f 2 -g 8
# Expected: ~450 GB/s bus bandwidth per GPU on 8-GPU DGX
