🚀 CI/CD Pipeline — GitHub Actions for GPU-Accelerated Django

Automate GPU model testing, Docker image building, and deployment with a CI/CD pipeline. GPU runners are expensive — use CPU runners for linting/unit tests, and GPU runners only for model validation.

YAML — .github/workflows/gpu-ci.yml
name: GPU CI/CD Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  # Stage 1: Fast linting & unit tests (CPU runner — FREE)
  lint-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: '3.11' }
      - run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - run: ruff check . && black --check .
      - run: pytest tests/unit/ -v --cov

  # Stage 2: GPU model validation (self-hosted GPU runner)
  gpu-model-test:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, gpu, a100]  # Your DGX or GPU server
    needs: lint-and-test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Verify GPU available
        run: nvidia-smi && python -c "import torch; assert torch.cuda.device_count() >= 1"
      - name: Load model & run validation
        run: |
          python manage.py warmup_models
          python tests/gpu/test_model_accuracy.py  # Accuracy > 0.85
          python tests/gpu/test_inference_latency.py  # P95 < 50ms
      - name: Export model to TensorRT & validate
        run: |
          python scripts/export_tensorrt.py --model job_pipeline --precision fp16
          python tests/gpu/test_tensorrt_engine.py

  # Stage 3: Build & push Docker image
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: gpu-model-test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: docker build -t registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Push to registry
        run: |
          docker login registry.anihpj.com -u ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USER }} -p ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_PASS }}
          docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:${{ github.sha }}

  # Stage 4: Deploy to K8s (ArgoCD or kubectl)
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: build-and-push
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - name: Update K8s deployment image
        run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-django \
            django=registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:${{ github.sha }} \
            -n anihpj-prod
          kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj-django -n anihpj-prod

🏗️ Infrastructure as Code — Terraform for GPU Clusters

Provision GPU cloud instances declaratively. This Terraform snippet creates an A100 GPU instance on AWS with the NVIDIA GPU Operator pre-configured.

HCL — terraform/gpu-cluster.tf
# ============================================================
# anihpj GPU Infrastructure — AWS p4d.24xlarge (8× A100)
# ============================================================

terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" }
    helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm", version = "~> 2.0" }
  }
}

# GPU Instance — p4d.24xlarge = 8× A100 40GB, 96 vCPU, 1.1TB RAM
resource "aws_instance" "gpu_training" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.nvidia_gpu_ami.id  # NVIDIA GPU-optimized AMI
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
  count         = var.training_nodes

  # GPU-optimized EBS volumes
  root_block_device {
    volume_type = "gp3"
    volume_size = 200  # GB
    iops        = 16000
    throughput  = 1000  # MB/s
  }

  # NVMe instance store for high-speed scratch
  # 8× 1TB NVMe SSDs included with p4d.24xlarge

  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.gpu_cluster_sg.id]
  subnet_id              = aws_subnet.gpu_subnet.id

  user_data = templatefile("${path.module}/scripts/gpu_init.sh", {
    cluster_name = var.cluster_name
    nfs_endpoint = aws_efs_file_system.models.dns_name
  })

  tags = {
    Name        = "anihpj-gpu-${count.index}"
    Environment = var.environment
    GPU_Type    = "A100-SXM4-40GB"
    GPU_Count   = "8"
  }
}

# EFS for shared model storage (all GPU nodes access same models)
resource "aws_efs_file_system" "models" {
  performance_mode = "maxIO"  # High throughput for model loading
  throughput_mode  = "bursting"
  tags = { Name = "anihpj-model-registry" }
}

# FSx for Lustre — high-performance parallel storage for training data
resource "aws_fsx_lustre_file_system" "training_data" {
  storage_capacity   = 4800  # 4.8 TB
  deployment_type    = "SCRATCH_2"  # Optimized for throughput
  subnet_ids         = [aws_subnet.gpu_subnet.id]
  security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.gpu_cluster_sg.id]
}

# GPU Node IAM — access to ECR (NGC), S3 (datasets), CloudWatch (logs)
resource "aws_iam_role" "gpu_node" {
  name = "anihpj-gpu-node-role"
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect = "Allow"
      Principal = { Service = "ec2.amazonaws.com" }
      Action = "sts:AssumeRole"
    }]
  })
}

# Output GPU instance IPs for Ansible inventory
output "gpu_ips" {
  value = aws_instance.gpu_training[*].private_ip
}

Appendix E: NVIDIA Glossary — 100+ Terms Defined

📖 A-Z REFERENCE

Every acronym, term, and concept from the NVIDIA ecosystem defined in plain English. This glossary is your quick-reference companion for the NCA-AIIO exam and daily work with NVIDIA infrastructure.

A — Ampere to Attention

Ampere: NVIDIA GPU architecture (2020). A100, 3rd-gen Tensor Cores, TF32, MIG, sparsity. Compute capability 8.0.
Attention Mechanism: The core operation in Transformers. Computes relevance scores between tokens. Computationally expensive — accelerated by Tensor Cores.
Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP): Training technique that uses FP16 for compute and FP32 for accumulation. 2× faster training with minimal accuracy loss.

B — Blackwell to Bus

Blackwell: NVIDIA GPU architecture (2024). B200, 5th-gen Tensor Cores, FP4, 20 PF AI. Named after mathematician David Blackwell.
Base Command Manager (BCM): NVIDIA's cluster management software. Job scheduling, user management, GPU provisioning.
Bandwidth: Data transfer rate. HBM3: 3.35 TB/s. NVLink: 900 GB/s. InfiniBand NDR: 400 GB/s.

C — CUDA to cuQuantum

CUDA: Compute Unified Device Architecture. NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and programming model. Foundation of GPU computing.
CUDA Core: Basic processing unit for integer and FP32/FP64 arithmetic. H100 has 14,592 CUDA Cores.
cuDNN: CUDA Deep Neural Network library. Optimized primitives for convolutions, pooling, normalization.
cuBLAS: CUDA Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms. GPU-accelerated matrix multiplication (GEMM).
cuQuantum: SDK for GPU-accelerated quantum circuit simulation.

D — DCGM to DPU

DCGM: Data Center GPU Manager. Telemetry, health monitoring, diagnostics for NVIDIA GPUs in data centers.
DGX: NVIDIA's purpose-built AI appliance. Pre-configured server with 8 GPUs, NVSwitch, InfiniBand, optimized storage.
DLI: Deep Learning Institute. NVIDIA's training and certification program.
DPU: Data Processing Unit (BlueField). Offloads infrastructure tasks (networking, storage, security) from CPU.

E — ECC to Exclusive Mode

ECC Memory: Error Correcting Code. Detects and corrects memory errors. Essential for HPC and AI training (prevents silent data corruption).
Embarrassingly Parallel: Problem that can be split into many independent tasks. GPUs excel at these. Matrix multiplication is embarrassingly parallel.
Exclusive Mode: GPU compute mode where only one process can use the GPU at a time. Set via nvidia-smi -c 1.

F — FP8 to FLOPS

FP8: 8-bit floating point. Introduced with Hopper (H100). Doubles throughput vs FP16 for AI inference.
FP16: 16-bit half precision. 2× faster than FP32 with minimal accuracy loss. Standard for deep learning training.
FP32: 32-bit single precision. Standard for scientific computing. Higher accuracy than FP16.
FP64: 64-bit double precision. Required for HPC/scientific workloads. A100/H100 have dedicated FP64 Tensor Cores.
FLOPS: Floating Point Operations Per Second. Measure of compute performance. H100: 1,979 TFLOPS FP8.

G — Grace to GPUDirect

Grace CPU: NVIDIA's ARM-based CPU (72 cores, 960 GB/s LPDDR5X bandwidth). Designed for AI workloads.
Grace Hopper Superchip (GH200): Grace CPU + Hopper GPU on one module. NVLink-C2C at 900 GB/s. Coherent memory.
GPU Operator: Kubernetes operator that automates GPU driver, runtime, and monitoring deployment.
GPUDirect: Technology for direct data transfer between GPU memory and third-party devices (NICs, storage) — bypassing CPU memory.

H — HBM to Hyper-Q

HBM: High Bandwidth Memory. Stacked DRAM providing massive bandwidth. HBM3: 3.35 TB/s on H100. HBM3e: 8 TB/s on B200.
HGX: NVIDIA's GPU baseboard. 4-GPU or 8-GPU configurations. Used by OEMs (Dell, HPE) to build AI servers.
Hopper: NVIDIA GPU architecture (2022). H100, 4th-gen Tensor Cores, FP8, Transformer Engine, DPX instructions.
Hyper-Q: Allows multiple CPU threads/processes to launch work on a single GPU simultaneously (32 hardware queues).

I — InfiniBand to INT8

InfiniBand: High-performance interconnect for HPC/AI clusters. NDR400 (400 GB/s), XDR800 (800 GB/s). RDMA support.
INT8: 8-bit integer quantization. 4× faster than FP32 for inference. TensorRT uses INT8 for maximum throughput.
Inference: Using a trained model to make predictions. Typically requires less compute than training. Optimized with TensorRT.

J — Jetson to JIT

Jetson: NVIDIA's edge AI platform. Orin modules for robots, drones, and IoT. Runs CUDA + TensorRT at the edge.
JIT (Just-In-Time): Compilation at runtime. CUDA uses JIT to compile PTX to GPU-specific binary. Numba's @cuda.jit compiles Python to PTX at runtime.

K — Kernel to K8s

Kernel (CUDA): A function that runs on the GPU. Launched with <<<grid, block>>> syntax. Thousands of threads execute the same kernel.
Kubernetes (K8s): Container orchestration. GPU Operator enables GPU scheduling. Resource: nvidia.com/gpu: 1.
KV Cache: Key-Value cache in Transformer inference. Stores attention keys/values to avoid recomputation. Major memory consumer in LLM serving.

L — L40S to LSTM

L40S: Data center GPU based on Ada Lovelace architecture. 48GB GDDR6, 1,466 TFLOPS FP8. Best perf/$ for inference.
Latency: Time to complete one inference request. Critical metric for real-time applications. P95 latency target: <10ms for anihpj.
LLM: Large Language Model. GPT-4, Llama 3, Nemotron. Trained on massive text corpora. Served via Triton + TensorRT-LLM.

M — MIG to Model Parallelism

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU): Partition an A100/H100 into up to 7 independent GPU instances. Each has dedicated memory, cache, and compute.
Mixed Precision: Using FP16 for forward/backward passes and FP32 for weight updates. Standard practice for DL training.
MMLU: Massive Multitask Language Understanding. Standard LLM benchmark covering 57 subjects.
Model Parallelism: Splitting a model across multiple GPUs. Required when model exceeds single GPU memory.

N — NCCL to NVTX

NCCL: NVIDIA Collective Communications Library. Optimized multi-GPU/multi-node communication primitives (all-reduce, all-gather, broadcast).
NGC: NVIDIA GPU Cloud. Container registry and model hub for GPU-optimized software.
NIM: NVIDIA Inference Microservice. Pre-built, optimized containers for deploying AI models.
NVAIE: NVIDIA AI Enterprise. Production-grade AI software suite with enterprise support.
NVTX: NVIDIA Tools Extension. Annotation library for marking code regions in Nsight profiles.

O — Occupancy to OOM

Occupancy: Ratio of active warps to maximum warps per SM. Higher = better latency hiding. Calculated as active_warps / max_warps.
Omniverse: NVIDIA's platform for 3D collaboration and digital twins. Uses USD (Universal Scene Description) format.
ONNX: Open Neural Network Exchange. Interchange format for ML models. Export from PyTorch/TF, deploy on Triton.
OOM (Out of Memory): Fatal GPU error when allocation exceeds available VRAM. Fix: reduce batch size, use gradient checkpointing, or enable MIG.

P — PCIe to PyTorch

PCIe: Peripheral Component Interconnect Express. Connection between CPU and GPU. Gen5: 64 GB/s (x16). NVLink is 14× faster.
Persistence Mode: Keeps NVIDIA driver loaded even when no apps are using GPU. Reduces latency. nvidia-smi -pm 1.
PTX: Parallel Thread Execution. NVIDIA's intermediate assembly language between CUDA C++ and GPU machine code.
PyTorch: Most popular deep learning framework. Native CUDA support. .cuda() moves tensors to GPU.

Q — Quantization to Queue

Quantization: Reducing model precision from FP32 to INT8/FP8/INT4. Reduces memory and increases throughput. TensorRT and bitsandbytes are common tools.
QLoRA: Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation. Fine-tune LLMs on a single GPU by quantizing to 4-bit and adding trainable adapters.
Quantum-2: NVIDIA's 400 GB/s InfiniBand switch platform. 64 ports, 51.2 Tb/s aggregate bandwidth.

R — RAPIDS to RTX

RAPIDS: Suite of GPU-accelerated data science libraries. cuDF (DataFrames), cuML (ML), cuGraph (graph analytics).
RDMA: Remote Direct Memory Access. Network adapter reads/writes GPU memory directly — no CPU involvement.
Register File: Fastest GPU memory. 65,536 × 32-bit registers per SM. More registers/thread = lower occupancy.
RTX: NVIDIA's ray tracing technology. RT Cores accelerate ray-triangle intersections. Omniverse rendering uses RTX.

S — SM to SuperPOD

SM (Streaming Multiprocessor): The building block of NVIDIA GPUs. H100 has 132 SMs. Each SM contains CUDA Cores, Tensor Cores, registers, and shared memory.
Sparsity: Technique to skip zero-valued weights. Ampere+ Tensor Cores support 2:4 structured sparsity for 2× throughput.
SuperPOD: NVIDIA's reference architecture for large-scale AI clusters. 32+ DGX nodes, InfiniBand fabric, validated design.

T — Tensor Core to Triton

Tensor Core: Specialized hardware unit for matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA). The heart of AI acceleration. 4th Gen on H100 supports FP8, FP16, TF32, FP64.
TensorRT: NVIDIA's inference optimization SDK. Layer fusion, kernel auto-tuning, precision calibration (FP32→FP16→INT8).
TF32: TensorFloat-32. 19-bit format using FP32 range + FP16 precision. 8× faster than FP32 on A100 with no code changes.
Triton: NVIDIA's multi-framework inference server. Supports PyTorch, TF, ONNX, TensorRT, custom backends. Dynamic batching.

U-V — USD to VRAM

USD (Universal Scene Description): Pixar's 3D interchange format. Omniverse uses USD as its native format.
vGPU: Virtual GPU. Shares a physical GPU across multiple VMs. Used for VDI, cloud gaming, and multi-tenant AI.
VRAM: Video RAM. GPU's onboard memory. H100: 80 GB HBM3. Consumer GPUs use GDDR6/GDDR6X. Critical for model size.

W-Z — Warp to Zero-Copy

Warp: Group of 32 threads that execute in lockstep on an SM. Fundamental unit of GPU execution. Divergence within a warp serializes execution.
XID Error: NVIDIA GPU fatal hardware error. XID 48 = double-bit ECC. XID 74 = NVLink error. XID 79 = GPU fell off bus. GPU replacement indicator.
Zero-Copy: Technique where GPU directly accesses host (CPU) memory over PCIe/NVLink. Avoids explicit cudaMemcpy. Lower bandwidth than device memory.

📝 NCA-AIIO Exam: 15 Must-Know Terms

These terms appear in 80%+ of NCA-AIIO exam questions. Master them first: CUDA (parallel computing platform), Tensor Core (MMA hardware unit), NVLink (GPU-to-GPU interconnect at 900 GB/s), MIG (GPU partitioning for multi-tenancy), HBM (high-bandwidth GPU memory), SM (Streaming Multiprocessor — the GPU building block), Occupancy (active warps / max warps), NCCL (multi-GPU communication), TensorRT (inference optimizer), FP8 (Hopper's 8-bit AI precision), InfiniBand (cluster interconnect), DCGM (GPU telemetry), Triton (inference server), DGX (AI appliance), and Grace Hopper (CPU+GPU superchip).

🛠️ Practical Terms Every GPU SRE Uses Daily

Beyond the formal glossary, these are the terms you'll hear in GPU infrastructure meetings, Slack channels, and incident calls:

GPU Lingo in Production

GPU Hung: GPU stopped responding. Usually requires reset (nvidia-smi -r) or power cycle.
GPU Starvation: GPU is idle because CPU can't feed data fast enough. Fix: increase batch size, use async data loader.
GPU Fragmentation: Multiple small jobs leave GPU memory fragments — can't fit a large job even though total free memory is sufficient. MIG helps.
Thermal Throttling: GPU automatically reduces clock speed to prevent overheating. Indicates cooling failure.
ECC Storm: Sudden spike in ECC error corrections. Often precedes a memory bank failure. Watch for XID 48.

MLOps & Infra Slang

Cold Start: First inference after model loads — slow because GPU memory is cold. Warm-up requests fix this.
GPU Bin Packing: Fitting multiple workloads onto one GPU to maximize utilization. MIG or MPS (Multi-Process Service).
Model Bloat: Model grew too large for GPU memory after fine-tuning. Fix: quantization, pruning, or bigger GPU.
GPU Fleece: Cloud provider charges for GPU but delivers degraded performance (throttled, shared, or older-gen). Verify with nvidia-smi.
N+1 GPU Redundancy: Keep one spare GPU per cluster for failover — not capacity. Hot spare vs cold spare.

Performance Terminology

Roofline Model: Visual tool showing if your kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound. The "roof" is peak FLOPS and peak memory BW.
Arithmetic Intensity: FLOPS / bytes accessed. High AI = compute-bound (Tensor Cores help). Low AI = memory-bound (need better caching).
Tail Latency: P99/P99.9 latency. The slowest 1% of requests. GPU inference tail latency often caused by batch padding or CPU-GPU sync.
GPU-Day: One GPU running for 24 hours. Standard unit for measuring AI compute cost. "That experiment cost 80 GPU-days on A100."

Infrastructure Acronyms

BOM: Bill of Materials — complete parts list for a GPU server/cluster.
MTBF: Mean Time Between Failures. GPU MTBF ~3-5 years. NVSwitch MTBF ~5-7 years.
TOPS/W: TOPS per Watt. Energy efficiency metric. H100: ~3 TOPS/W (1,979 TOPS / 700W).
GPU TCO: Total Cost of Ownership. Hardware + power + cooling + maintenance + support over 3-5 years.
SLA: Service Level Agreement. NVAIE includes 24/7 support SLA. Open-source = no SLA (you're on your own at 2 AM).

📋 NCA-AIIO Exam Day Checklist

✅ Before the Exam

• Schedule exam 2-4 weeks out for focused prep time
• Review all 345 questions in this guide — know the explanations
• Take 3 timed mock exams (90 min each) — aim for 80%+
• Memorize: GPU specs table, NVCC -arch flags, DCGM commands
• Test your Pearson VUE system 48 hours before
• Prepare ID (must match registration name exactly)

❌ During the Exam — Avoid

• Don't spend > 2 min on any question — flag and return
• Don't second-guess your first answer unless certain
• Don't leave any question unanswered (no penalty for guessing)
• Don't get stuck on performance-based questions
• Don't use external resources (proctored — no notes)

🧪 Hands-On Practice

NVIDIA DLI: Free GPU cloud labs for courses.
Google Colab: Free T4 GPU (limited). Good for learning.
Lambda Labs: Rent A100/H100 by the hour.
vast.ai: Peer-to-peer GPU rental. Cheapest for practice.

🏆 Exam Time Strategy

• 0-10 min: Skim all. Answer easy ones (~30%)
• 10-60 min: Work medium. Flag hard (~50%)
• 60-80 min: Return to flagged. Eliminate wrong options.
• 80-90 min: Review all. Verify no blanks. Submit.

🆓 How to Get Free GPU Credits

• Google Cloud: $300 free credit for new accounts (90 days). Enough for ~200 hrs of A100.
• AWS Activate: Up to $100K in credits for startups. Includes GPU instances.
• Azure for Startups: Up to $150K in credits. Includes ND A100 v4 instances.
• NVIDIA Inception: Free for AI startups. Cloud credits, hardware discounts, technical support.
• Academic Programs: NSF ACCESS (US researchers), XSEDE — free GPU hours for research.

📋 Registration Process

1. Create account at nvidia.com/certification
2. Select exam → Pearson VUE checkout
3. Choose: Online proctored (OnVUE) or Test center
4. Online: Test your system 48 hrs before. Need webcam, quiet room, no dual monitors.
5. Test center: Arrive 30 min early with 2 forms of ID.
6. Results: Immediately after exam (provisional pass/fail).
7. Badge: Credly digital badge within 48 hrs of passing.

🏆 Final Words — The Journey Continues

You've completed 33 chapters, 345 practice questions, and 6 comprehensive appendices. You understand GPU architecture from the transistor level to the data center scale. You can write CUDA kernels, deploy models on Triton, design GPU clusters, and monitor infrastructure with DCGM.

But more importantly, you understand why accelerated computing matters. It's not just about faster computation — it's about solving problems that were previously impossible. Drug discovery, climate modeling, autonomous vehicles, and generative AI all depend on the technology you now understand deeply.

"Accelerated computing is the path forward. The more you buy, the more you save." — Jensen Huang

Now go build something that matters. The GPU clusters are waiting. 🚀
